problem: Step 7 miscounts. With p true there are 4 rows (q and r free), and p→q forces q = T in 2 of them, not 1. Saying '1 row sets q true' gives the right final answer of 1 row by accident and teaches a wrong counting step.
fix: step 7: Keep only rows where p is true: 4 rows. In each of those, p→q forces q = T, which leaves 2 rows (q = T, r still free). step 8: With q = T, q→r forces r = T, so exactly 1 row satisfies all three premises, namely p = T, q = T, r = T.

where: Section 3 (last paragraph) and Exam traps, first bullet
problem: 'Only MP and MT squeeze information out of an implication' and 'only modus ponens and modus tollens are valid for an implication' contradict the chapter's own table, where hypothetical syllogism, constructive dilemma and destructive dilemma are valid forms built on implications. A student can read this as saying HS is invalid.
fix: Say instead: of the rules that use one implication together with one of its parts, only MP (from p) and MT (from ¬q) are valid; HS, CD and DD are also valid but combine two implications or add a case split.

problem: 'the contrapositive of p→q used backwards' is vague and can be misread as using the converse, which is invalid.
fix: MT applies modus ponens to the contrapositive: p→q is equivalent to ¬q→¬p, so from ¬q we get ¬p.
